summary: Describes the pNFS block or volume layout, which lets clients directly access file data on block storage, bypassing the NFSv4 server for data transfers to increase performance and parallelism.

plainLanguage.summary: Parallel NFS lets a client read or write file data directly on block storage. The NFS server supplies a map and controls when clients may use it.

questions: what is the pnfs block layout
what is an extent in pnfs
how does pnfs fence a client
what is copy on write in pnfs
subtitle: Clients map NFS file ranges to storage blocks and read or write them directly.

tldr.problem: Ordinary NFS sends file data through its server. pNFS lets clients reach storage directly, but block storage needs a precise map and careful coordination.
tldr.mechanism: The server gives clients layouts made of extents, each mapping a file range to a volume range and stating which I/O is allowed.
tldr.outcome: Clients can transfer data directly and in parallel, but must enforce file permissions and stop using expired layouts. RFC 6688 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 5663 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2010. It has been updated by RFC 6688.

sections.title: Direct Access to Block Storage
sections.content:
Parallel NFS (pNFS) lets clients access file data on storage without sending every data operation through the NFS server. RFC 5663 defines the block and volume layout used with storage based on blocks, including SCSI-family protocols.

The server coordinates access and supplies layout information. Clients use that information to reach the storage directly; the server-to-storage control protocol is outside this document's interoperability scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The server tells a client where the file data is stored. The client then transfers that data directly to or from the storage system.

sections.title: Volumes and File Extents
sections.content:
A volume is a sequence of fixed-size blocks, such as a logical disk. It may be a physical disk, part of one, or a combination of volumes arranged as slices, concatenations, or stripes.

A layout maps parts of a file to byte ranges on volumes. Extent offsets and lengths use 64-bit values. Extents MUST align to 512-byte boundaries; writable extents MUST also align to the server's file-system block size.
sections.plainLanguage: A volume is storage divided into fixed-size blocks. A layout tells the client which volume range contains each part of a file.

sections.title: Finding and Describing Volumes
sections.content:
Clients identify a simple volume by matching byte-string signatures at specified offsets, rather than relying on network addresses. A signature can have up to 16 components, and a negative offset counts from the end of the volume.

The server describes complex volumes as an indexed topology of simple volumes, slices, concatenations, and stripes. The topology's root is the last array element. A device identifier can name the complete topology returned by GETDEVICEINFO.
sections.plainLanguage: A storage system may have several network paths, so the client recognizes a volume by its contents. The server can describe a larger volume as a structure built from simpler ones.

sections.title: Extent States and Permissions
sections.content:
Each extent identifies a volume, a file offset and length, a storage offset, and a state. READ_WRITE means valid data may be read or written; READ means valid data may only be read; INVALID means allocated space is not initialized; NONE means a hole with no storage location.

Reads from INVALID or NONE extents return zeroes. A write to INVALID storage changes the written range to READ_WRITE and the client reports that change with LAYOUTCOMMIT. Extents are permissions: a client MUST NOT perform direct I/O that its current layout does not allow.
sections.plainLanguage: Each extent says whether its data can be read, written, is not initialized, or has no storage. The client must follow that permission and report newly written data to the server.

sections.title: Copy-on-Write and Layout Safety
sections.content:
For copy-on-write, a writable layout can include read-only data and matching invalid extents. A partial-block write reads the old block, merges the change, and writes the result to the invalid extent. Later reads use the new writable data.

Servers coordinate layouts with locks and reservations. When storage does not make overlapping operations atomic, the server MUST use one writer or multiple readers. Layouts expire with the NFS lease; a client must stop using an expired layout. Without communication confirming that the client stopped, the server waits the lease time plus the client's maximum I/O time before transferring layouts.
sections.plainLanguage: For a partial change, the client combines the old data with the new bytes and writes a new block. A layout also expires, so clients must stop using it on time.

sections.title: Client Responsibilities and Security
sections.content:
Storage access controls commonly distinguish hosts, not individual file blocks. A server may fence a host from a volume, but it generally cannot stop a client from accessing blocks outside its layout or blocks in a layout it returned.

Clients must enforce layout limits, NFS locks, access-control lists, and file open modes. The RFC says block/volume layouts SHOULD NOT be used when clients cannot be trusted to enforce these rules or when the storage protocol cannot meet the required security.
sections.plainLanguage: The storage system may not know which file a block belongs to. The client must obey the server's map and enforce file-level access rules.

items.label: READ_WRITE
items.desc: Valid data; reading and writing are allowed.

items.label: READ
items.desc: Valid data; reading only is allowed.

items.label: INVALID
items.desc: Allocated but uninitialized storage; reads return zeroes.

items.label: NONE
items.desc: A file hole with no physical storage.
